messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Vignette:
Michael, a 34-year-old European American firefighter, came to treatment after several months of feeling increasingly on edge in ways that surprised even him. He had always thought of himself as someone who could handle pressure, and for years his work had confirmed that self-image. What changed was a deployment as a relief worker in a war zone, where he spent weeks moving through damaged streets, helping to carry the injured and dead, and trying to remain useful in places where ordinary rules of safety no longer seemed to apply. He did not describe a single dramatic turning point so much as a series of moments that lodged in his mind: entering buildings whose entrances were half-collapsed, waiting in tense silence for permission to move, watching unfamiliar people approach quickly in the street while he tried to judge whether they were asking for help or bringing danger. When he returned home, those scenes followed him in a way that made ordinary places feel subtly altered. The first time he walked into his own kitchen after returning, he found himself pausing automatically to look toward the doors and windows, as if he needed to learn where he could get out if something changed. That habit soon spread. Michael said that whenever he entered a room, whether at the fire station, a grocery store, or a family gathering, his eyes went first to the exits. He did it without meaning to, almost before he registered where he was, and he became uneasy if he could not immediately identify a way out. Even at home, where he had once felt completely at ease, he found himself sitting in places that let him stay close to a door. He chose the end of the couch, angled toward the hallway, and at restaurants he preferred tables near the entrance. He explained that being far from an exit made him feel trapped in a way he could not dismiss.

Since the deployment, Michael had also become markedly wary of strangers approaching him in everyday situations. A person stepping toward him on the sidewalk, a man coming up too quickly in a parking lot, or someone asking him for directions with unexpected urgency could make his body tense before he had time to think. He said he knew these were ordinary encounters, but he no longer experienced them as ordinary in his body. Instead, he watched the distance between himself and other people, noted their hands, their pace, and where they were looking. He did not describe acting aggressively, but he was careful and pulled back when he could. At work, this showed up in small but noticeable ways. As a firefighter, he was used to crowded scenes and unfamiliar faces, yet now he found himself checking the room as soon as he entered a station meeting, a training room, or a community event. He would stand where he could see the doorway and feel more settled if he knew who was coming and going. He had not stopped working, but he was more guarded in spaces he could not quickly read.

At home, the change was just as evident. Michael told his wife that he felt on guard even inside his own house, something he found embarrassing and difficult to explain. Nighttime was especially hard because he was aware of sounds that he had once ignored: a car slowing outside, footsteps on the sidewalk, the creak of a branch near the window. He was not frightened in a dramatic way; rather, he described a steady readiness, as if part of him expected the world to become dangerous without warning. He would check the locks more than once and then sit with his attention split between whatever he was doing and the sense that he needed to stay prepared. The strain of this had accumulated over time in his marriage, not as a single conflict but as a quiet narrowing of his life. He declined invitations that involved crowded places, and although he still went to work, he found himself choosing positions that let him see entrances and keep movement around him predictable.

Michael also described a loss of ease around feeling good. After the war-zone deployment, moments that should have felt comforting or joyful could suddenly make him uneasy, and he had learned to push them away. He would notice himself beginning to relax with his wife or feel a brief lift after a good shift, and then he would intentionally shut it down, as though positive feeling was too exposed a place to stand. He said it made him feel vulnerable, almost foolish, and he preferred to stay emotionally braced rather than let himself settle into contentment that might be interrupted. He was not detached from the people he loved, but he had become cautious about letting himself enjoy being close or happy.

He also stopped exercising in the way he used to. Before the deployment, he had run and lifted weights regularly, partly for fitness and partly because it helped him decompress from the demands of firefighting. Now he avoided it. The physical intensity of exercise felt too close to the sensations he had lived through overseas: elevated heart rate, breathlessness, the feeling of being physically primed for danger. Rather than pushing through, he let the routine slide, and over the weeks he found himself less anchored in the habits that had once structured his days. By the time he sought help, his score on a PTSD measure reflected a moderate level of distress, but what brought him in was less the number than the sense that he was no longer comfortable in the places that had once been most familiar to him. He came because he wanted to feel safer at home, to stop scanning every room for exits, and to be able to move through ordinary life without bracing for strangers or having to hold back his own moments of relief. What frightened him most was the possibility that this guarded way of living had become permanent, and what he hoped for was a way to return to his wife, his work, and his own home without feeling as if he were always waiting for something to happen.
